# High bird body temperatures aided adaptive radiation

- Birds maintain body temperature of 40° C through *endothermy*---metabolic production of heat
- Higher than all other reptiles, mammals, and amphibians 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/body_temp.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Moreira et al. 2021)

# Air sacs facilitate respiration 

- Thin-walled, non-vascular compartments throughout body cavity and cervical vertebrae 
- 6 (in weavers) to 12 (shorebirds and storks)
- Connected to lungs by **secondary bronchi** 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/airsac.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_anatomy#Respiratory_system))

# Air sacs facilitate respiration 

- Air sacs expand and contract with entire abdominal cavity
- Forces air through rigid lungs

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/respiration.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_anatomy#Respiratory_system))

# Unidrectional airflow in bird lungs maximizes $O_2$ transfer 

- No residual air left in lungs during ventilation 
- More efficient gas exchange 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/cross_exchange.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_anatomy#Respiratory_system))

# Birds have a four-chambered heart

- 2-4% of body mass (verus <1% in small mammals)
- Typically 150-350 bpm (1200 bpm in hummingbirds)
- Lower resting heart rate than similarly sized mammals
- High blood pressure!

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/heart.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)

# Thermoregulation

- Endotherms must cope with metabolic heat in hot environments and heat loss in cold environments
- Can make physical adjustments, phsyiological changes, and behavior

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/pterocles.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [*Pterocles alchata*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/34143601)

# Metabolism 

- **Basal metabolic rate** / BMR: energy expenditure when resting
- **Active metabolic rate**: energy expenditure when active 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.4\linewidth]{images/bmr.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Tommy Norin](https://www.sebiology.org/events/animal-satellite-2022.html))

# Birds have high basal metabolic rate

- High relative to most vertebrates

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/scaling.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Tommy Norin](https://www.sebiology.org/events/animal-satellite-2022.html))

# Birds have high metabolic scope

- **Metabolic scope** = active metabolism / resting metabolism
- Especially high in running birds

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/metabolic_scope.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Bundle et al. 1999)

# Low energy expenditure for temperature regulation in thermoneutral zone

- $T_{LC}$: Lower critical temperature
- $T_{UC}$: Upper critical temperature

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/tnz.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Bozinovic et al. 2014)

# Which statement is most correct?

a) BMR can be measured in a resting bird below $T_{LC}$
b) BMR can be measured in an active bird above $T_{LC}$ and below $T_{UC}$
c) BMR can be measured in a resting bird above $T_{LC}$ and below $T_{UC}$
d) BMR can be measured in a resting bird above $T_{UC}$
d) BMR can be measured in an active bird below $T_{LC}$

# Plumage impacts metabolic temperature regulation

- Summer plumage less insulative than winter plumage in Willow Ptarmigan, requires higher BMR for a given temperature

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/willow_ptarmigan.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([ML93964071](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/93964071); Speakman et al. 2010)

# Hypothermia

- **Nocturnal hypothermia**:  $T_{body}$ drops 8-10° C to conserve energy (doves, pigeons, vultures, some passerines)
- **Torpor**: $T_{body}$ drops >10° C, reduce respiratory rate (1-2x per minute versus 300-400 in hummingbirds), reduce heart rate (30 bpm versus 500), reduce energy consumption 10-60%

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/anhu_snow.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([C.J. Battey](http://cjbattey.com/))

# Torpor helps Andean hummingbirds cope with altitude 

- Blue and purple lines individual $T_{body}$ measurements
- Dashed blue line ambient temperature

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/torpor.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Wolf et al. 2020)

# Why is the duration of torpor bout inversely correlated with body mass loss?

a) birds in torpor burn fewer calories
b) birds in torpor lose less water to the atmosphere through respiration
c) birds in torpor have greater metabolic scope
d) a & b
e) a, b, & c

# Hibernation

- Common Poorwills drop temperature from 106° F to 65° F for 2-3 months
- "Discovered" in 1946, but Hopi Indian name (*Hölchko*) means "The Sleeping One“!

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/poorwill.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [*Phalaenoptilus nuttallii*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/164513671)

# Meriwether Lewis on poorwills (1806)

> It appeared to be passing into the dormant state.…the bird could scarcely move. I run [sic] my penknife into its body under the wing and completely destroyed its lungs and heart yet it lived upwards of two hours. This fanominon [sic] I could not account for unless it proceeded from want of circulation of the blood 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.2\linewidth]{images/lewis.jpg}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriwether_Lewis)

# Hyperthermia

- Birds can reduce $T_{body}$ by respiration: **panting** (evaporative cooling of nasal, buccal, pharynx regions) and **gular flutter** (special pant via vibrating hyoid muscles / bones in throat; targets mouth and upper respiratory tract)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.4\linewidth]{images/gular.png}
\end{figure}  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3_Ft32uEuaA

\hfill \tiny (Bartholomew et al. 1968) 

# Physiology informs climate change predictions

- Snow Buntings have high cold tolerance at cost of reduced heat tolerance 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/bunting_climate.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([ML63891021](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/63891021); O'Connor et al. 2021) 

# Avian digestion

- **Proventriculus** secrets mucus, HCl + pepsinogen (converted to protein-digesting **pepsin**) to chemically digest food 
- **Gizzard** (ventriculus): muscular avian equivalent of molars, with keratinized lining + sometimes grit
- **Crop**: expanded esophagus chamber that stores and softens food + regulates flow

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/gizzard_2.jpg}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Colorado State](https://vivo.colostate.edu/hbooks/pathphys/digestion/otherspp/birds.html))

# Water balance

- Evaporative water loss high per unit mass in small birds
- Partially offset by **metabolic water** production (enhanced by high avian metabolisms)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/water_loss.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Bartholomew & Cade 1963) 

# Excretion

- Kidneys concentrate nitrogenous wastes as **uric acid** (0.5-1 mL $H_2O$ to excrete 370 mL N versus 20 mL in mammals) 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/poop.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Natural History Museum](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/do-birds-pee.html))

# Avian osmoregulation

- Birds lack loops of Henle used by mammalian kidneys for salt excretion 
- Seabirds drink seawater (3% salt versus 1% salt in body fluids), must excrete through **nasal salt glands**

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/salt_glands.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Cornell](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/news/why-can-some-birds-drink-salty-seawater/))
